title: [Short Paper] Forensic Analysis of Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Agents
threat_model: Indirect prompt injection against LLM agents that ingest external content. The paper takes a post-hoc forensic stance: the attack has already occurred and the question is whether it can be reconstructed from agent execution logs.
technical_summary: A digital-forensic framework for LLM agents: it generates agent execution logs on a realistic agentic-task benchmark, then uses LLMs to analyse those logs and identify traces of indirect prompt injection. The contribution is the forensic pipeline and benchmark rather than a defense.

title: Embedding-Based Detection of Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models Using Semantic Context Analysis
technical_summary: Proposes an embedding-based detector for Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks that works by analysing the semantic relationship between the user's stated intent and the external content retrieved into context, rather than by inspecting the external content in isolation. That relational framing is the paper's core idea: an injected instruction is anomalous not because of its own surface features but because it is semantically unrelated to what the user asked for, which is a signal a content-only filter cannot see. The method is deliberately architecture-agnostic - it sits outside the LLM as an external detection layer requiring no modification to the model, in contrast to prevention-focused approaches that alter the underlying architecture. title: Secure Prompt Engineering Patterns for Cloud LLM Agents
threat_model: Direct and indirect prompt manipulation of cloud-integrated LLM agents holding varying privilege levels, aiming at unauthorized cloud operations, data exposure, privilege escalation and resource misuse. Testbeds use isolated projects with controlled access rights and logging.

title: ProjGuard: Safety Monitoring for Computer-Use Agents via Low-Dimensional Projections
threat_model: Computer-use agents operating real desktop operating systems, exposed to prompt injection, indirect instructions and visual attacks delivered through the environment they observe.
technical_summary: A behavioural-trajectory safety monitor for computer-use agents: instead of inspecting prompts or inputs with a second model, it derives a scalar risk signal from the agent's accumulated interaction history at each step and checks online whether execution is drifting toward an unsafe region of a low-dimensional projection.

technical_summary: Introduces a multimodal prompt-injection technique that embeds malicious instructions inside a mind map image rather than in text, exploiting a property specific to that visual format: mind maps are intentionally incomplete, consisting of nodes and branches without explanatory detail. technical_summary: A three-way ensemble detector for prompt injection - supervised classifier, zero-shot LLM inference and rule-based heuristics - released together with two purpose-built cybersecurity prompt-injection datasets and a systematic review of the Scopus-indexed literature.

title: TraceCaps: Inline Provenance and Risk Enforcement for Agentic Software Engineering

technical_summary: Formalizes 'context rot' as a system-level failure class in production LLM agents - the progressive degradation of reasoning quality, task coherence and decision fidelity arising from uncontrolled accumulation, misalignment and entropic decay of context across extended agentic sessions - and argues it is architectural rather than model-specific. Memory-anchored reasoning grounds each inference step to retrieved passages through explicit citation tokens, producing an auditable reasoning chain rather than an unsupported answer - so provenance is a structural property of generation rather than a post-hoc attribution. Causal intervention probes identify hallucination-prone attention patterns by measuring the counterfactual impact of context perturbations, targeting the Lost in the Middle phenomenon specifically; this is a genuinely diagnostic method, since perturbing context and observing output change establishes which positions actually influence the answe

title: Alleviating Contextual Misguidance: Response-Aware Prompt Compression for Long-Context Question Answering
technical_summary: Diagnoses a specific cause of Lost in the Middle and proposes a targeted mitigation. The paper's analytical contribution is the identification of 'contextual misguidance': the failure to retrieve centrally-located information is often caused not by position alone but by query-relevant yet non-grounding segments that distract the model - passages that look topically related to the query and therefore attract attention, without containing the information needed to answer it. That is a sharper mechanism than generic positional bias, and it connects Lost in the Middle to the distraction-by-irrelevant-context mechanism in this corpus's registry, arguing they are aspects of the same failure rather than separate phenomena. title: Cognitive Scaffold: From Fluid Context to Crystallized Memory for Long-Horizon DeepResearch Agents
technical_summary: Introduces Cognitive Scaffold, a factorized memory architecture for long-horizon DeepResearch agents, targeting what the authors name the 'context-noise trade-off': linear accumulation of interaction history degrades reasoning and dilutes fine-grained evidence, so simply keeping everything is self-defeating. The architecture decouples the agent's cognitive state into two components - a Fluid Working Context serving immediate reasoning, and a persistent Knowledge Graph for long-term retention - so that what the model attends to now is separated from what the system remembers. title: FocusAgent: Simple Yet Effective Ways of Trimming the Large Context of Web Agents
threat_model: The security evaluation (Section 6) targets indirect prompt injection attacks against web agents, where malicious instructions are embedded in page content that is not visible to the human user but is present in the textual AxTree observation the agent processes -- specifically banner attacks (malicious instructions inserted into SVG elements and their alt-text fields) and popup attacks (a popup containing hidden malicious text embedded in the AxTree). The attacker is assumed to control content on a visited web page (e.g., via a compromised or malicious site element) and aims to hijack the agent's action sequence to pursue the attacker's goal instead of the user's task goal, evaluated using the DoomArena framework on WebArena Reddit tasks; the paper does not consider attacks that manipulate the retriever itself (e.g., adversarially crafting content to survive the LLM-based pruning step)
technical_summary: FocusAgent addresses the dual problem of context bloat and prompt-injection vulnerability in LLM-based web agents by using a lightweight LLM (e.g., GPT-4.1-mini) as a step-wise retriever over accessibility-tree (AxTree) observations, rather than relying on embedding/BM25-based chunk retrieval or naive bottom-truncation, both of which the authors argue either underperform in zero-shot settings or risk discarding essential contextual information. title: Multi-Route Search and Adaptive Fusion for Power QA with Small Language Model Guidance
technical_summary: Proposes a multi-path adaptive fusion retrieval framework guided by small language models for power-system documentation question answering, where documents serve as the core guideline for safe grid operation and retrieval precision bears on grid stability. Three domain-specific failure modes motivate it, each an instance of a mechanism in this corpus's registry: semantic drift from non-standardized industry terminology; increased semantic noise from fixed-window segmentation, i.e. chunking that cuts across the document's logical structure and produces fragments whose meaning depends on removed context; and knowledge conflicts arising in multi-source retrieval. The framework addresses these in sequence. It first constructs a common terminology repository and a section-structure-aware index that preserves the physical hierarchical logic of the source documents - so chunking follows docume

title: Preemptive Answer "Attacks" on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
threat_model: Two variants are studied side by side. In the unintentional case there is no attacker at all: the user's own prompt phrasing ('first give an answer, then show the step-by-step solution') causes the model to emit an answer before reasoning. In the malicious case a user performs prompt injection to force the same answer-first ordering with an attacker-chosen answer. The attacker needs only prompt-level access and no model internals.
technical_summary: Introduces the preemptive answer scenario, in which an LLM produces an answer before it reasons, and shows that the subsequent chain-of-thought degrades to rationalizing that answer rather than deriving one. Distinguishes an unintentional variant arising from ordinary answer-first prompt phrasing from a malicious variant induced by prompt injection, and measures both with accuracy and an attack success rate across six reasoning datasets, two models and three CoT methods. Finds the incidental and adversarial variants inflict comparable damage on arithmetic tasks, which makes this one of the few papers in the corpus to instrument both failure modes under one protocol. Proposes two lightweight mitigations, problem restatement and self-reflection, which reduce but do not remove the degradation.

title: BenchOverflow: Measuring Overflow in Large Language Models via Plain-Text Prompts
threat_model: Deliberately weak: any ordinary user issuing natural-language requests, with no adversarial suffixes, jailbreaks, special tokens, model-specific artifacts, corpus control or model access. The paper frames Overflow as arising from helpfulness priors and absent length control, so it can be triggered inadvertently (student misuse, curiosity stress tests) or exploited at scale for compute amplification, cost inflation (denial-of-wallet) and cross-tenant service degradation.
technical_summary: Introduces Overflow, a non-adversarial failure mode in which ordinary plain-text prompts elicit excessive generation, and BenchOverflow, a model-agnostic benchmark of nine prompting strategies that amplify output volume without adversarial suffixes or policy circumvention. Evaluates nine open- and closed-source models under a standardized protocol with a fixed 5,000-new-token budget, quantifying tail risk with cap-saturation rates (CSR@1k/3k/5k) and empirical CDFs, and analysing within-prompt variance and cross-model correlation. Positions Overflow against optimized resource-exhaustion attacks (Engorgio, AutoDoS, OverThink, BitHydra) by requiring no optimization or data control. Assesses a lightweight model-agnostic conciseness reminder as a first-line mitigation and shows it attenuates right tails unevenly across models and strategies.

title: You've Changed: Detecting Modification of Black-Box Large Language Models
threat_model: The defender is a downstream developer consuming a black-box LLM through an API with no visibility into provider-side changes. The 'adversary' is either a provider performing silent updates, model swaps, quantization changes or control-vector edits, or a party injecting text into the system prompt. The paper highlights a class of injection in which the target task is not replaced but a distributional property of responses (for example sentiment) is shifted, leaving individual responses looking normal.
technical_summary: Proposes monitoring a black-box LLM for modification by comparing distributions of linguistic and psycholinguistic features of its generated text across time, using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests (with Bonferroni correction when aggregating features) to decide whether two samples came from the same model. Evaluates discrimination across five OpenAI completion models, identifies which feature families carry the signal, and measures sensitivity on synthetic mixtures of text from two models. Extends the same machinery to a secondary question: whether a system-prompt injection that shifts the sentiment distribution rather than replacing the task can be detected, using 3,000 Llama 3 70B book reviews per condition and VADER sentiment. Frames the method as a cheap continuous alternative to benchmark re-evaluation, which is expensive and vulnerable to benchmark contamination.

title: KVEraser: Learning to Steer KV Cache for Efficient Localized Context Erasing
threat_model: N/A - not an adversarial-attack defense in the classic sense; the paper targets a general 'context erasing' problem where a short span already written into the KV cache is later identified as stale (out-of-date retrieved facts), incorrect (a faulty tool observation), retracted (a withdrawn user preference), or harmful (an adversarial instruction/injection in an imported skill file), and the system must make future decoding behave as though that span never appeared, without full recomputation.
technical_summary: Introduces KVEraser, a learned KV-cache editing method that performs efficient, localized 'context erasing': given a processed context and a span to remove (e.g., a stale retrieved fact, an incorrect tool observation, a retracted user preference, or a harmful injected instruction), it replaces only that span's cached KV states with learned steering states while reusing the rest of the cache unchanged, avoiding the suffix-length-dependent cost of full recomputation. Trains a two-stage pipeline (generic span-neighbor pre-training, then task-specific fine-tuning) on Qwen3-8B and evaluates against full recomputation and three approximate baselines (delete-and-shift, instruction-only forgetting, local suffix repair) on a controlled synthetic erasing benchmark (1K-32K context) and on unseen long-document QA with harmful factual distractors, achieving near-full-recomputation quality at a fracti

title: A pen mark is all you need - Incidental prompt injection attacks on Vision Language Models in real-life histopathology
threat_model: Deliberately weak: the central claim is that NO attacker is required. Handwritten pen marks, diagnostic annotations and institutional watermarks are routinely present on real pathology slides, so ordinary clinical data acts as an unintentional injection carrier. The authors contrast this with classical VLM prompt injection, which 'requires an active malicious actor with access to the prompt itself'. A malicious variant (deliberately swapped prostate/ovary watermarks) is also tested.
technical_summary: Evaluates whether ordinary, non-adversarial artifacts on histopathology slides - handwritten pen labels, diagnostic annotations and institutional watermarks - function as unintentional prompt injections for vision-language models. Constructs four clinically relevant tasks (T-stage, lymph node infiltration, mutational status, tissue of origin) over public TCGA and TCIA whole-slide images and varies whether the visible label leaks the truth, misleads, or is absent, for 3888 total observations across three frontier VLMs. Finds the models abandon the tissue entirely and read the label: near-perfect on truth-leaking labels, near-zero on misleading ones, versus 30-65% clean baselines. Tests prompt engineering as a mitigation and shows it fails, with GPT-4o even moving in the opposite direction. title: Privacy-Preserving Prompt Injection Detection for Smart Cloud-Deployed Large Language Models
threat_model: Cloud LLM providers want to retroactively audit historical user prompts for newly discovered prompt-injection templates without storing raw user text, which may contain sensitive personal/business information subject to privacy regulation.
technical_summary: Proposes a privacy-preserving prompt injection detection scheme for cloud-deployed LLMs that combines salted hash-based exact matching with sentence-embedding-based near-match detection over sliding-window chunks of user prompts, so raw plaintext is never persistently stored. Adds an optional blockchain logging layer (tested on the Sepolia testnet) for tamper-evident audit trails of flagged prompts. Benchmarks the scheme against full-text embedding detection and window-based hash detection on 2,000 synthetic test prompts spanning four injection templates, showing consistently higher F1 across similarity thresholds and window sizes. Concludes the approach balances detection accuracy with strict privacy requirements.

title: Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine: A Zero-Trust Security Gateway for Enterprise LLM Systems
threat_model: Attackers submit arbitrary prompts (prompt injection, encoded payloads, multi-step reasoning attacks) without access to internal system settings or model configuration, attempting credential theft, role escalation, or confidential-document extraction from an enterprise LLM deployment across Admin/Employee/Intern access levels.
technical_summary: Introduces the Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine, a Zero-Trust AI Security Gateway that enforces input sanitization, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), adversarial prompt detection, and deterministic tokenization of sensitive entities before prompts reach an enterprise LLM. Evaluates the gateway on a 300-prompt adversarial subset derived from the HackAPrompt benchmark across five attack categories under three RBAC roles. Reports 98.7% block accuracy and 99.3% tokenization accuracy versus 82%/75% for an unprotected baseline LLM deployment, with only a modest latency increase. Identifies usability trade-offs from default-deny policies and dependence on detection-model accuracy as open limitations.

title: Securing With Dual-LLM Architecture: ChatTEDU an Open Access Chatbot’s Defense
threat_model: Anonymous public users interact with an open-access, multilingual RAG-based educational chatbot and attempt prompt injection, jailbreaking, content manipulation, spam/advertisement insertion, and denial-of-service-style exploitation; 77.8% of observed real attacks used technical exploitation (vs. content-based manipulation) and 15% involved multilingual attack attempts.
technical_summary: Introduces ChatTEDU, a dual-LLM defense architecture for an open-access, multilingual RAG-based educational chatbot deployed at TED University. Separates content moderation (LLM-1, GPT-4 with few-shot prompt-engineered threat classification) from response generation (LLM-2, GPT-4), so the moderation model gates all input before the generation model ever processes it. Evaluated against 4,501 real-world production interactions (180 malicious) collected over a two-month deployment, achieving 100% detection of identified attacks with 0.28% false positives and only 18% latency overhead while sustaining 95% throughput under peak concurrent load. Acknowledges that no baseline defense was directly compared on the same dataset and recommends future standardized benchmarking.
